name: Curaçao Papiamentu
confidence_why: Remijsen & van Heuven 2005 and Rivera-Castillo & Pickering 2004 both call Papiamentu stress lexically distinctive (e.g. 'mata 'to kill' vs ma'ta 'killed', irregular nouns like 'hoben, 'aguila), and Kouwenberg & Murray 1994 report exactly the same placements but prefer to call the system quantity-sensitive and predictable 'with few exceptions', so the facts are agreed and only the label is argued.

catalog_quote: Curaçao Papiamentu has both lexically distinctive stress and, independently, a word-level tone contrast. ... In verbs, the location of primary stress is predictable from the number of syllables and the morphological category. The vast majority of disyllabic verbs have penultimate stress in the base form. ... In the corresponding participle forms (1b), however, stress is on the final syllable. ... Longer verbs uniformly have final stress, both in the base form and in the participle ... In nouns, adjectives and adverbs – i.e. in all lexical categories other than verbs – stress is to some extent predictable from syllable weight, with closed syllables counting as heavy. That is, stress is on the penultimate, unless the final syllable is heavy, in which case the final syllable is stressed, as shown in (2). ... sweep_summary: Papiamento (papi1253) is in the catalog as 'lexical' on Remijsen & van Heuven 2005. the list of works with stress in the title holds three distinct works (seven Glottolog records, all already listed). (1) Remijsen & van Heuven 2005: downloaded the open Leiden postprint (hdl:1887/14092) and read §2.2.1-2.2.3; the catalog quote is verbatim from p. 207 and the paper states stress is lexically distinctive (disyllabic verb base penult vs participle final; non-verbs weight-sensitive penult/final with many irregular final/penult/antepenult exceptions) — confirms. (2) Kouwenberg 2007 (already held by the project, OA): pronoun-clitic paper whose §2.2 restates the system as category-predictable (verbs final H, 3+-syllable verbs final stress, disyllabic verbs trochaic penult stress with final H; non-verbs quantity-sensitive right-edge trochee) — refines, consistent with the catalog. (3) Rivera-Castillo 1998 (JPCL 13(2): 297-334): closed at John Benjamins (Unpaywall/OpenAlex/S2 all closed, no repository copy); only the publisher's first-page preview image (title + abstract) was obtainable and. the abstract claims four basic lexical patterns of tone and stress with stress dependent on tone; Kouwenberg 2004 (pp. 61-62, Table 4) and R&vH 2005 (p. 211) summarize it as requiring lexical H placement and an independent stress prosodeme — consistent with 'lexical', medium acquisition priority since R&vH 2005 already supersedes it. Extra: Kouwenberg 2004 (held by the project, OA, not a works with stress in the title) read for its Table 1 and 'Stress placement in verbs' section — refines. No source contradicts the catalog; best statement remains R&vH 2005 §2.2.1, now verified from a saved copy. access checks were done by automated download, Unpaywall, OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar and Crossref APIs.

new_statements.reading: Curaçao Papiamentu word stress is lexically distinctive (minimal pairs 'mata 'to kill' vs ma'ta 'killed'; irregular nouns 'hoben, li'he, 'aguila) but largely rule-governed within categories: disyllabic verbs penult (participle final), verbs of 3+ syllables final; non-verbs penult unless the final syllable is closed, with many lexifier-inherited exceptions including antepenult. Secondary stress alternates from the primary. This is the catalog's deciding source, now verified first-hand from the open Leiden postprint; the catalog_quote is verbatim from p. 207 and the 'lexical' coding stands.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Papiamentu has two level tones H and L alongside stress. The authors argue (p. 12) that 'with few exceptions, the placement of H and main stress in Papiamentu words can be predicted from categorial class membership and syllable weight'. Verbs: stress depends on syllable count - bisyllabic verbs always have penultimate (initial) stress with H on the final syllable (H and stress do not coincide, e.g. kaska 'peel', mata 'kill'); trisyllabic and longer verbs have final H and final stress (kuminsá 'begin'); monosyllabic verbs trivially final. Nouns, adjectives, adverbs: weight-sensitive - final H and stress if the final syllable is heavy (rhyme with at least two weight units, e.g. falis 'suitcase', karèt 'currant'), penultimate H and stress if the final syllable is light (buraku 'hole'). Words ending in l,r,n after schwa (òrgel, sténdert) count as light because the final rhyme is a syllabic sonorant. Participles of bisyllabic verbs shift H and stress to the final syllable (fadá 'tired'). Roughly 250 bisyllabic minimal pairs differ by tone melody alone (HL vs LH) with the same penultimate stress (papa 'porridge' vs papa 'father'). Phonetic correlates: loudness plus optional lengthening on L-toned stressed syllables of bisyllabic verbs; loudness plus high pitch in longer verbs.
new_statements.secondary_stress: 'Secondary stress is assigned to alternating syllables; we will not discuss it.' (p. 13). In longer verbs 'We either find L on all preceding syllables, or alternating HL: speakers which have the latter pattern realise secondary stress as H.' (p. 13). Per Römer (1991: 47) some speakers have (L)HLL on irregular-antepenult words, others (L)HLH, 'secondary stress - which is assigned to alternating syllables - is realised by the latter class of speakers as H' (p. 14).
new_statements.exceptions: p. 14: 'Genuine exceptions are of the following kinds: (i) words with H and stress on the wrong syllable, i.e. either on a final light syllable, or on an (ante)penultimate syllable where the final syllable is heavy; (ii) words in which the placement of H is irregular.' Examples (7): irregular final stress karnisá 'pickled meat', mashá 'very', muhé 'woman'; antepenultimate ásido 'acid', rápido 'fast', idéntiko 'identical'; penultimate difísil 'difficult', mártir 'martyr'; (8) irregular melody ónzebar 'poltergeist', mucha 'child', tambe 'too, also'. Bisyllabic verbs with irregular HL melody (4): sunchi, skeiru, feter, beitel, wèlder, freta, fangu (all Dutch or English origin). Inherited compounds (bistek, failkast) have H on adjacent syllables (§1.3.6). Nouns formed with autostressed -dó and with -mentu retain base stress; adjectives in -bel have penultimate stress. Noun/verb pairs differ by tone shift or stress shift (§2.5.1.2-4).
new_statements.identity_note: Kouwenberg & Murray 1994 describe Papiamentu of all three ABC islands, not the Curaçao dialect alone: they adopt Curaçaoan spelling ('We have adopted the Curaçaon spelling for this description of Papiamentu, except where in chapter 4 examples are quoted from Aruban sources', p. 4), state that 'There are some dialectal differences among the three islands, but the dialects are mutually [intelligible]' (p. 4-5), and used native-speaker consultants from both Curaçao and Aruba (p. 5). Their tone facts are drawn largely from Römer (1977, 1991) and Dijkhoff (1993), i.e. Curaçao-based work, so the stress description is compatible with the catalog's Curaçao Papiamentu entry (Glottolog papi1253 covers Papiamento as a whole).

new_statements.quote: Treatments of Papiamentu stress have assumed it to follow an Iberian pattern, and the orthography reflects this. Regular stress is thought to be penultimate for words ending in a vowel or l,r,n, final for words ending in another consonant or a diphthong. In words that do not conform to this pattern the placement of stress is marked in the orthography by an acute. This creates an immediate problem for the treatment of verbs: all trisyllabic and longer verbs end in a vowel and have final stress. These are thus treated as an open-ended class of exceptions, although their behaviour is fully predictable.

readall_conflicts: No factual disagreement between Kouwenberg & Murray 1994 and the catalog's deciding source Remijsen & van Heuven 2005: both give bisyllabic verbs penultimate stress, verbs of three or more syllables final stress, participles final, non-verbs penultimate unless the final syllable is heavy (closed), with lexical exceptions including antepenult and alternating secondary stress. The only difference is framing: the catalog codes the system as lexically distinctive (minimal pairs such as 'mata vs ma'ta, irregular nouns), while Kouwenberg & Murray argue that 'with few exceptions' stress placement is predictable from categorial class and syllable weight and describe the language as quantity-sensitive (they note it 'has not previously been recognised as a quantity-sensitive language', p. 12); they also state that the traditional Iberian-style rule (penult after vowel or l,r,n, final otherwise) is wrong for verbs. Both sources agree that tone (H/L melodies) is a separate, lexically contrastive layer that carries about 250 bisyllabic minimal pairs with identical stress. Rivera-Castillo & Pickering 2004 could not be opened (host gone, the Internet Archive unreachable), so nothing from it can be weighed.

sources.note: Curaçao Papiamentu has lexically distinctive stress and, independently, a privative word-level tone contrast. Verbs: disyllabic base = penult stress, participle = final stress (mata/matá), 3+ syllables final in both. Non-verbs: weight-sensitive (penult unless final syllable closed), with many lexifier-inherited exceptions (final, penult, antepenult: 'hoben, li'he, 'aguila). Secondary stress on alternating syllables. §2.2.3: 'Stress is distinctive in most disyllabic verbs, where it distinguishes the base form from the participle.' The catalog_quote is verbatim from p. 207.

The fully predictable nature of high tone and stress placement in verbs ... the bisyllabic verb base combines penultimate stress with a LH melody, whereas the trisyllabic derived verb has a final stressed and high-toned syllable' (pp.56-57); 'in nouns, adjectives, and adverbs, stress placement is sensitive to the weight of the final syllable' (p.57; final schwa+/l,r,n/ counts light: binager, òrgel penult vs fabor, os

sources.note: Table 1 (after Kouwenberg & Murray 1994:12): disyllabic verbs final H + penult stress; longer verbs final H + final stress; non-verbs with heavy final syllable final H + final stress, light final syllable penult H + penult stress. Participles (matá) and some nouns (piská, ágila, difísil) are irregular and carry a lexically pre-associated H that attracts stress. Argues stress/tone are largely predictable from category and weight, with a closed set of lexically marked exceptions.

sources.quote: The description of the interdependence of tonal and stress features in Papiamentu provides important insights on the genesis of mixed creole systems in which these suprasegmental features are phonologically distinctive. The present account represents a constraint-based and feature-based analysis that [...] proposes that tone and stress are directly related. This paper includes (a) a description of four basic lexical patterns of tone and stress in Papiamentu, (b) a discussion of problems that alternative analyses face when dealing with mixed systems, and (c) a principled way to explain relations between suprasegmental features.
sources.note: The main formal (OT, foot-based) analysis of Papiamentu stress placement, summarized second-hand in Kouwenberg 2004 Table 4; relevant if the record's 'lexical vs weight-predictable' framing is ever contested.
